variants.name: Container reference (std::string& / std::vector<T>&)
variants.idiom_name: reference to a standard container with append/push_back
variants.implementation_notes: The collector object collapses into a reference to a standard container: producers take `std::string&` or `std::vector<T>&` and call `append`/`push_back`/`insert`, and the caller owns the container end to end. Standard containers grow geometrically, so appends are amortised constant time, and the pattern needs no helper class at all. Prefer returning a value when there is a single producer; use an out-reference when a call tree must contribute into one container (text generation, tree flattening, visitation).
pitfalls: The reference is an unadvertised output: the signature no longer says the value changes - name it `out`/`into` and document the append order.
Any iterator, pointer or reference into the container is invalidated when `push_back` reallocates: cppreference documents that all iterators and element references are invalidated on reallocation.
A dangling reference if the accumulator is a temporary or dies before the last producer runs (for example work handed to a detached thread or a stored callback).

variants.name: Stream accumulator (std::ostream& with operator<<)
variants.implementation_notes: The accumulator is an `std::ostream&`: producers overload `operator<<(std::ostream&, const T&)` and the caller decides whether the sink is an `std::ostringstream` (collect into a string), an `std::ofstream` (collect into a file) or `std::cout`. This is the C++ form of the pattern for formatted text and it extends to third-party types through ADL without touching them. In C++20, `std::format_to(std::back_inserter(s), ...)` is the allocation-light successor for formatted appends.
pitfalls: `operator<<` must return the stream; returning void breaks chaining and stream manipulators.
Formatting state (width, fill, flags, precision) is sticky: a producer that mutates the stream's flags changes how every later producer appends.
Exception and locale settings live on the stream, so an `ostringstream` configured to throw can turn a failed append into a throw at an unexpected place in the call tree.

variants.name: Output iterator (std::back_insert_iterator / std::back_inserter)
variants.implementation_notes: When producers are generic algorithms or templates that cannot know the concrete container, hand them an output iterator instead: `std::back_inserter(out)` wraps `push_back` behind the iterator protocol, so `std::copy`, `std::generate_n` or a custom `OutputIt` producer appends into the caller's container (assignment through the iterator appends; increment is a no-op). This is the c2 wiki's own 'output iterator' reading of the collecting parameter and it composes with ranges, e.g. `std::ranges::copy(xs, std::back_inserter(out))`. Prefer it for library-style producers; prefer a container reference for application code that can name the type.
pitfalls: A back-insert iterator can only be written through; producers that must read the accumulated state need a container reference instead.
Passing `out.begin()` rather than `std::back_inserter(out)` writes over existing elements instead of appending.
Insertion can reallocate the container: any other iterator into the same container held during the call is invalidated.
